cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK VII
The palace and gardens of Alcinous;\nArete's question.
So he prayed there, much-enduring noble Odysseus,\nwhile the mules' strength carried the girl to the city.
And when she reached her father's famous house,\nshe halted at the gateway; and her brothers around her
stood, men like the immortals, and from under the wagon\nthey loosed the mules, and carried the clothing in;
and she herself went to her room. And her fire was lit
by an old woman of Apeire, the chamber-keeper Eurymedusa,\nwhom once the curved ships brought from Apeire:
they had picked her out as a prize of honor for Alcinous,
because he ruled all the Phaeacians,\nand the people listened to him as to a god.
She had nursed white-armed Nausicaa in the halls,
and now she kindled her fire\nand made her supper in her room.
And then Odysseus rose to go to the city; and Athena,
with kind thought for Odysseus,\npoured a thick mist around him,
so that no great-hearted Phaeacian, crossing his path,\nmight needle him with words and ask him who he was.
But when he was on the point of entering the lovely city,\nthere the goddess, gray-eyed Athena, met him,
in the likeness of a young girl,\nunwed, carrying a pitcher.
She stopped in front of him, and noble Odysseus asked her:
"Child, would you not guide me to the house of a\nman named Alcinous, who is lord among these people?
I am a stranger, hard-worn, come here from far away,\nout of a distant country: so I know not one
of the people whose city and land this is."
Then the goddess spoke to him again, gray-eyed Athena:
"Then I will show you,\nfather stranger, the house you bid me
show: for he lives close by my own blameless father.
Only go in silence, so, and I will lead the way:
do not look at any of the people, and ask no questions.
For these men do not much endure strangers,\nnor welcome with open love the man who comes from elsewhere.
They trust instead in their fast ships, their swift ones,
and cross the great gulf on them,\nsince the earth-shaker granted it:
ships swift as a wing, or as a thought."
So speaking, Pallas Athena led the way swiftly,\nand he followed in the footsteps of the god.
And the Phaeacians, famed for ships, never marked\nhim going through the city among them: Athena
of the lovely braids would not\nallow it — the dread goddess —
who poured a wondrous haze around him,\nwith kind thought in her heart.
And Odysseus wondered at the harbors and the trim ships,
at the gathering-places of the\nheroes themselves, and the walls,
long and high, fitted with palisades, a wonder to see.
But when they came to the king's famous house,\nthe goddess, gray-eyed Athena, began to speak among them:
"Here, father stranger, is the house you bid me\nshow you. You will find the Zeus-nurtured kings
feasting at the feast. Go in, and let your heart\nfear nothing: the bold man proves the better man
in every venture, though he come from another country.
First you will come upon the mistress in the halls:
Arete is the name she is called, and she comes of the same
parents, the very ones who fathered King Alcinous.
Nausithous first was born from Poseidon the\nearth-shaker and Periboea, loveliest of women,
youngest daughter of great-hearted Eurymedon,\nwho once was king over the overweening Giants —
but he destroyed his reckless people,\nand was destroyed himself.
With her Poseidon lay, and fathered a son,\ngreat-hearted Nausithous, who ruled among the Phaeacians;
and Nausithous fathered Rhexenor and Alcinous.
Rhexenor — still without a son, a bridegroom in his hall —
Apollo of the silver bow struck down, leaving one\nonly child, Arete. Her Alcinous made his wife,
and honored her as no other woman on earth is honored,
of all the wives who now keep house under their husbands:
so heartfelt is the honor she has held, and holds still,\nfrom her dear children and from Alcinous himself
and from the people, who look on her as on a god
and greet her with blessings\nwhen she walks through the town.
For she herself has no lack of noble understanding:
for those she favors — even men — she dissolves quarrels.
If she once takes kindly thought for you in her heart,
then there is hope you will see your own people, and come
to your high-roofed house and your own fatherland."
So speaking, gray-eyed Athena went away over\nthe barren sea, and left lovely Scheria,
and came to Marathon and wide-wayed Athens,\nand entered the close-built house of Erechtheus. But Odysseus
went toward the famous house of Alcinous, and his heart
was churning as he stood there,\nbefore he reached the threshold of bronze.
For there was a sheen as of the sun or the moon through\nthe high-roofed house of great-hearted Alcinous.
Walls of bronze ran this way and that,
from the threshold to the inmost room,\nwith a frieze of blue enamel round them;
doors of gold closed the close-built house within;
the doorposts standing on the\nbronze threshold were of silver,
the lintel above was silver, and the door-handle gold;\nand on either side stood dogs of gold and silver
that Hephaestus had made with his knowing craft\nto guard the house of great-hearted Alcinous —
creatures deathless and unaging all their days.
And within, seats stood along the wall this way and that,
from the threshold to the inmost room\nin an unbroken line, and over them
were thrown fine close-spun coverings, the work of women.
There the leaders of the Phaeacians would sit\ndrinking and eating: what they had never failed.
And youths of gold on well-built pedestals\nstood holding blazing torches in their hands,
lighting the nights through the house for the feasters.
And fifty slave-women serve the house:
some grind the apple-gold grain at the mill,\nothers weave at the looms and turn the spindles,
sitting close as the leaves of a tall poplar,\nand from the close-woven linen the soft oil runs.
As far as the Phaeacian men are skilled beyond all others
at driving a fast ship on the sea, so are their women
masters of the loom: for Athena has given them beyond\nothers knowledge of beautiful work, and noble minds.
And outside the courtyard,\nclose by the doors, is a great orchard
of four acres, with a hedge driven round it on both sides.
There tall trees grow in full leaf and flower:
pears and pomegranates and apple trees bright with\nfruit, sweet figs and olives in full flourish.
Their fruit never perishes, never fails,\nwinter or summer, the year round; but always
the breathing West Wind sets some growing, ripens others:
pear grows old upon pear, apple upon apple,\ngrape-cluster upon cluster, fig upon fig.
And there his vineyard, heavy with fruit, is rooted,\none part of it a drying-ground on level open earth,
baking in the sun; other grapes they are gathering,
and others they are treading;\nand out in front are the unripe ones,
one row shedding its blossom,\nanother darkening toward purple.
And there, by the last row of vines, grow ordered beds
of greens of every kind, shining the whole year through;
and two springs: one is scattered through all the garden,
the other dives under the courtyard threshold and runs
toward the high house,\nwhere the townsfolk drew their water.
Such were the shining gifts of\nthe gods in the house of Alcinous.
There much-enduring noble Odysseus stood gazing.
And when his heart had wondered at it all,\nhe stepped quickly over the threshold into the house.
He found the leaders and counselors of the Phaeacians
pouring from their cups to the sharp-eyed slayer of Argus,
to whom they poured last of all,\nwhen they thought of sleep.
But much-enduring noble Odysseus went on through the house
wrapped in the thick mist Athena had poured around him,\nuntil he came to Arete and to King Alcinous.
And Odysseus threw his arms around Arete's knees —
and then, just then,\nthe god-sent mist poured back off him.
And they fell dumb through the\nhouse at the sight of the man,
and stared in wonder. And Odysseus made his plea:
"Arete, daughter of godlike Rhexenor:
to your husband, to your knees, I come after much labor —
and to these feasters. May the gods grant them\nfortunate lives; and may each hand down to his children
the wealth in his halls, and the\nhonors the people have given him.
But for me — speed my sending,\nthat I may come to my fatherland,
and quickly: for long now,\nfar from my own people, I suffer pains."
So speaking he sat down on the hearth, in the ashes\nby the fire; and they were all hushed in silence.
At long last the old hero Echeneus spoke —\na man elder-born beyond the other Phaeacians,
who excelled in speech, knowing\nmany things grown old with him;
with good will toward them he spoke to the assembly:
"Alcinous, this is not the\nfairer way — it is not fitting —
a stranger sitting on the ground,\non the hearth, in the ashes,
while these men hold themselves in, waiting for your word.
Come — raise the stranger up, and seat him on\na chair with silver studs, and bid the heralds
mix more wine, so that to Zeus who delights in thunder
we may pour also — the god who\nwalks beside honored suppliants;
and let the housekeeper give the\nstranger supper from her stores."
And when the sacred strength of Alcinous heard it,
he took the hand of battle-wise Odysseus,\nthe man of shifting counsels,
raised him from the hearth and set him on a shining chair,\nmaking his son stand up — kind-hearted Laodamas,
who sat beside him, and whom he loved the most.
A handmaid brought water for their hands in a pitcher,
a beautiful golden one, and poured it over a silver basin
for them to wash, and drew up\na polished table beside them.
The grave housekeeper brought\nbread and set it before them,
laying out delicacies in plenty,\ngiving gladly of her store;
and he drank and ate, much-enduring noble Odysseus.
And then the strength of Alcinous said to the herald:
"Pontonous, mix the bowl, and serve out the wine to all\nin the hall, so that to Zeus who delights in thunder
we may pour also — the god who\nwalks beside honored suppliants."
So he spoke, and Pontonous mixed the honey-hearted wine
and served all, pouring first\ndrops in each cup for the gods.
And drunk what their hearts would have,\nAlcinous addressed them all, and said:
"Hear me, leaders and counselors of the Phaeacians,\nwhile I say what the heart in my breast commands.
Now you have feasted: go home and take your rest;\nin the morning we will call more of the elders together
and host the stranger in the halls, and offer the\ngods fine victims; and after that we will think also
of his sending, so that without\nlabor or pain this stranger
may come, under our escort, to his own fatherland\nrejoicing, and quickly, though he come from very far,
and suffer no evil or harm midway before he\nsets foot in his own land. There, afterward,
he will suffer whatever Destiny and the grave Spinners
spun in his thread at his birth, when his mother bore him.
But if he is one of the deathless ones,\ncome down from heaven,
then this is some new thing the gods are devising:
for always in time past the gods have shown themselves\nopenly to us, whenever we offer glorious hecatombs,
and they feast beside us, sitting where we sit.
And if a lone traveler on the road meets them,\nthey use no disguise with us — for we are of near kin,
like the Cyclopes and the wild tribes of the Giants."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Alcinous, let your mind be easy on that count.\nI am not like the deathless ones who hold wide heaven,
not in build, not in bearing: I am like mortal men.
Whoever you know among mankind who carry the heaviest
loads of misery — it is to them I would compare my pains.
Yes, and I could tell a still longer tale of evils,\nall that I have labored through by the gods' will.
But let me eat my supper, for all my grief:
for there is nothing more\ndog-shameless than the hateful belly,
which commands a man to remember it, by force,\nhowever worn he is, however deep the sorrow in his heart —
as I have sorrow in my heart, and still this thing\nforever bids me eat and drink, and makes me forget
all I have suffered, and orders me: be filled.
But you — bestir yourselves at the showing of dawn,\nto set me, unlucky as I am, on my own fathers' soil,
even after all I have suffered.\nAnd let life leave me once I have seen
my own possessions, my slaves,\nand my great high-roofed house."
So he spoke, and they all approved it and urged that\nthe stranger be sent home, since he had spoken rightly.
But when they had poured,\nand drunk what their hearts would have,
the others went home to sleep, each man to his own house,\nand noble Odysseus was left behind in the hall,
and beside him sat Arete and godlike Alcinous,\nwhile the handmaids cleared away the service of the feast.
And white-armed Arete began to speak among them —
for she had recognized the mantle\nand the tunic, seeing the beautiful
clothes she herself had made with her attendant women —\nand lifting her voice she spoke winged words to him:
"Stranger, this question first, and I ask it myself:
What man are you, and from where?\nWho gave you these clothes?
Did you not say you came here wandering over the sea?"
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"It is hard, my queen, to tell my griefs straight through
to the end: the gods of heaven have given me so many.
But this I will tell you,\nsince you ask it of me and inquire.
There is an island, Ogygia, lying far off in the sea,\nwhere the daughter of Atlas lives — guileful Calypso
of the lovely braids, a dread goddess;\nand no one mixes with her, no god, no mortal man.
But me — unlucky me — some power brought to her hearth
alone, after Zeus with a hurl of\nthe white lightning had shattered
my fast ship apart in the middle of the wine-dark sea.
There all the rest of my brave companions perished,\nbut I threw my arms round the keel of my curved ship
and was carried nine days;\nand on the tenth, in the black night,
the gods brought me near the island Ogygia, where Calypso
lives, she of the lovely braids,\nthe dread goddess. And she took me in
and loved me and tended me devotedly, and promised\nto make me deathless and unaging all my days;
but she never once persuaded the heart in my breast.
There I stayed seven years unbroken, and forever wet\nwith my tears the immortal clothing Calypso gave me.
But when the eighth year came wheeling round for me,\nthen at last she urged me — commanded me — to go,
whether by some message from Zeus,\nor her own mind had turned.
She sent me off on a raft bound\nplank to plank, and gave me much —
bread and sweet wine —\nand dressed me in immortal clothing,
and sent up a fair wind for me, harmless and warm.
Seventeen days I sailed on, crossing the water,\nand on the eighteenth appeared the shadowy mountains
of your land, and my own heart was glad — ill-fated\nas I was: for I was yet to keep company with misery
in plenty, sent upon me by Poseidon the earth-shaker,\nwho loosed the winds against me and barred my road,
and stirred up a sea past all speaking; nor would the wave
let me be carried on my raft, for all my thick groaning.
The squall then shattered the raft to pieces. But I
swam — cut my way across that gulf — until wind and\nwater carried me near, and brought me to your land.
There, as I climbed out, the wave\nwould have forced me onto the shore,
dashing me on the great rocks in a joyless place;\nbut I gave way, and swam back out, until I came
to a river, where at last the ground seemed best to me,
clear of stones, and there was shelter from the wind.
I dropped there, gathering my\nspirit back; and ambrosial night
came on. I climbed out clear of the heaven-fed river
and fell asleep in the bushes,\nand heaped the fallen leaves
around me; and a god poured down boundless sleep.
There in the leaves, my heart worn down with grief,\nI slept the whole night through, and dawn, and midday;
the sun was slanting down when sweet sleep let me go.
And I saw your daughter's handmaids on the beach\nat play, and she among them, like the goddesses.
To her I made my plea. And she did\nnot fail in noble understanding —
as you would not hope of the young when you meet them\nface to face: for the young are forever thoughtless.
She gave me bread in plenty, and fire-bright wine,\nand a bath in the river, and gave me these clothes.
That, for all my grieving,\nis the truth of it, told through."
Then Alcinous answered him in turn, and said:
"Stranger, in this one point, truly, my child did not see
rightly: that she did not bring\nyou with her attendant women
to our house — when she was the first you supplicated."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Hero, do not scold your blameless daughter for that.
She did tell me to follow along with her handmaids;\nit was I who would not — out of fear, out of shame,
lest perhaps your own heart darken at the sight:
we are jealous-minded things,\nwe tribes of men upon the earth."
Then Alcinous answered him in turn, and said:
"Stranger, the heart in my breast is not the kind
to take fire for nothing.\nDue measure is better in all things.
If only — father Zeus, Athena, Apollo! —\nbeing the man you are, and thinking as I think,
you would take my daughter and be called my son-in-law,
staying here: I would give you a house and possessions —
if you stayed willingly. Against your will no Phaeacian\nshall hold you: father Zeus forbid such a thing.
As for your sending, I appoint it — be sure of it —\nfor tomorrow. Till then you will lie mastered by sleep,
and they will row the calm, until you come
to your fatherland and your house,\nand whatever place is dear to you,
though it be far, much farther than Euboea —\nwhich those of our people say is farthest of all
who saw it, when they carried fair-haired\nRhadamanthus out to visit Tityus, the son of Earth.
They went all the way there,\nand finished it without strain,
and on the same day accomplished the journey home again.
And you shall know for yourself,\nin your own heart, how far my ships
are the best — and my young men at\nthrowing up the sea with the oar-blade."
So he spoke; and much-enduring noble Odysseus was glad,\nand he spoke in prayer, and said a word, and named:
"Father Zeus, may Alcinous accomplish all he\nhas said: on the grain-giving earth his fame
would be unquenchable —\nand I would come to my fatherland."
So the two of them spoke such things to one another,\nwhile white-armed Arete told her handmaids
to set out bedsteads under the porch, and to lay on\nthem beautiful purple blankets, and spread rugs above,
and fleecy cloaks on top of all, for cover.
Out of the hall they went with torches in their hands;
and when they had briskly spread the close-corded bed,\nthey came and stood beside Odysseus and called him:
"Up, stranger, come and sleep: your bed is made."
So they spoke; and welcome it seemed to him to sleep.
So he slept there, much-enduring noble Odysseus,\non a corded bedstead under the echoing porch;
but Alcinous lay down in the inner room of the high house,
where the lady his wife made ready his bed and his rest.
